summary: Alberta lookout site labelled EAGLE on the province's 2009 map; no public source found for its build date, staffing or state today.

events.note: Labelled as a lookout site on Alberta's 2009 lookout tower map (a map, not a register)

evidence.supports: The 2009 Alberta lookout tower map marks a lookout site called EAGLE.
Alberta's history of boreal lookouts says towers were built on high hills so the observer could see past obstacles.
evidence.quote: towers, built on high hills in the boreal forest, which elevated the observer over any obstacles to vision.

evidence.supports: Steel increasingly replaced wood for tower construction from the 1920s on.
evidence.quote: Introduced in the 1920s, steel increasingly replaced wood for tower construction.

evidence.supports: Some towers were slimmer, up to 18.3 m (60 ft) tall, with a small cupola lookout on top.
evidence.quote: Other towers were narrower, up to 60 feet high, with a small cupola lookout on top.

evidence.supports: The province counts 127 wildfire lookout sites.
evidence.quote: 127 wildfire lookout sites are located throughout

evidence.supports: Each lookout site is staffed by an observer who watches for wildfire all day, generally April to October.
evidence.quote: Each site is staffed by a lookout observer whose job is to watch for wildfire all day, each day, generally from April to October.

evidence.supports: Alberta's bear-safety guidance describes wildfire lookout sites as isolated.
evidence.quote: Wildfire lookout sites are isolated and the staff that work them must be prepared

evidence.supports: Permanent electric fencing has been installed at priority lookout sites, enclosing towers, outhouses and generator buildings.
evidence.quote: Permanent electric fencing has been installed at priority wildfire lookout sites, enclosing the residences, lookout towers, outhouses and generator buildings.

evidence.supports: Fence posts are painted in high-visibility colours to alert backcountry visitors to be cautious.
evidence.quote: High visibility painting on the fence posts alert backcountry visitors to be cautious year-long.

sources.title: Lookout towers map 2009
sources.publisher: Government of Alberta, Open Government (Sustainable Resource Development)

corrections.proposed: Site already on the 2009 map; a 2010 structure would be a rebuild or replacement, not the first build
corrections.why: The 2009 map labels a lookout site called EAGLE, so 2010 cannot be the site's first construction. The brief's note calls 2010 the present structure's year, which no public source I could read confirms.

notes_for_editor: Public sources give only the 2009 map label and the general Alberta lookout network; nothing public dates this tower or describes it today. The brief's 2010 build year, staffing and access are not supported by any source I could read; the year comes from the FIReS-derived WF_WILDFIRE_LOOKOUT layer, which its metadata marks Protected (need-to-know), and I used none of its records. A map-text fragment places an EAGLE label beside WHITECOURT, but the extraction is too garbled to use for location. Search results mentioned Eagle lookouts only outside Alberta (New Mexico, British Columbia, Wisconsin), which are not this site. Access left unset: no source describes public access.
